E1351.summary: Neoplatonist philosopher Atwood cites heavily in support of inward withdrawal, sudden divine Light, union with the source and pure Matter; the later Appendix qualifies his account of First Matter.
E1351.body: Named among the Alexandrian revival figures professing Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge [I.1 ¶27], and among the Neoplatonists whose surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶9]; Atwood calls him ‘the graceful Plotinus’ [II.1 ¶39]. She cites him in support throughout: on the same doctrine while condemning suicide [II.3 ¶37]; on the soul's participation of Deity, perceiving “that the supplier of life is present” [II.3 ¶46]; on the beauty of the gods seen through Intellect — “All the gods, says Plotinus, are beautiful, and their splendour is intense.” [II.4 ¶29; II.4 n17]; on the sudden arrival of the One: “He comes, says Plotinus, suddenly alone” [II.4 ¶50]. From the Select Works and Ennead 5 she takes the sudden Light of Intellect — “a sudden Light, and this Light is from Intellect, and is also It” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n31] — and approach to the universal subject through an image, a portion of gold [III.1 ¶32; III.1 n37]; and again “For the Light is with Power, and is God.” [IV.2 ¶41; IV.2 n28]. With Porphyry he is the source of her summary on the Subject of bodies, analysis and pure divine Matter, that “there should be a Nature primarily vital which is also formless, indestructible and immortal” [III.2 ¶46–49; III.2 n38–39]; n38 says he alludes to the mystical analysis. He supports knowledge of real beings by self-investigation, where “the reality is testified by reminiscence” [III.2 ¶50], and asks how the infinite is conceived — the Indefinite by the Indefinite [III.2 ¶53]; and inward conversion, union with Divine nature, the soul's middle order and the value of its fall from the treatise on the Descent of the Soul: “Often when by an intellectual energy, I am roused from body and converted to myself” [III.2 ¶50; III.2 n41]; union as experimental ingress requires that one “separate body from the man and its defilements” [III.2 ¶66]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is referred to on how pure matter is generated [APP ¶43] but qualified: he gives only the metaphysic of the First Matter's generation, never realized so — “a recessure of reason behind itself into the indefinite intermediate between reason and the Absolute” [APP ¶137].

E1352.summary: Author Atwood cites, as ‘well initiated in these mysteries’, on Chemia, the passions as impediments, the Moon and Sun, Typhon's names and the fable's meaning.
E1352.body: Atwood cites Plutarch for the etymology of Chemia: Egypt was called Cham/Chemia for its black soil, and “by the word Chemia, says Plutarch, the seeing pupil of the human eye was also designated” [I.1 ¶5]. From De Iside et Osiride, calling him ‘well initiated in these mysteries’, she takes support for senses and passions as impediments, the rites preparing the aspirant for knowledge of the Supreme Mind: “the souls of men are not able to participate of the Divine nature whilst they are thus encompassed about with senses and passions” [II.1 ¶50; II.1 n45]. He supports the Moon as reason and Wisdom, the Sun as force: “the influence of the Moon, says Plutarch, seems to reflect the works of reason” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n49]; he explains that Typhon's names Seth and Bebo import violent restraint, contrariety and subversion [III.1 ¶63]; and he is cited, with the Adepts, as witness to the fable's meaning [IV.2 ¶7].

E1353.summary: The soul's subtle vehicle which, when humid and condensed, presents apparitions to the inner sense.
E1353.body: Atwood speaks of “our pneumatic vehicle, becoming humid and condensed beneath her heaven” [II.3 ¶22]; in this state it presents apparitions to the inner sense, and the soul looking outward “beholds the shadow and images of her vaporous vehicle” [II.3 ¶27]. Whether the ‘vaporous vehicle’ is the same as the pneumatic vehicle is apparently implied by the context, not stated.

E1354.summary: The Divine Poemander of Hermes Trismegistus, praised for sublime doctrine and cited as testimony of the operative revelation of Intellect.
E1354.body: Atwood praises the Divine Poimander for sublimity of doctrine, though it concerns divine capabilities and regeneration rather than their physical ground [I.1 ¶7]. From book 2 she takes a testimony of the operative revelation of Intellect to which, she says, nothing can be added: “For the sleep of the body was the sober watchfulness of the mind” [III.3 ¶58; III.3 n36]. It supplies language for the real suffering passions cause in the revealed light — they “do force the inwardly placed man to suffer sensibly” [III.3 ¶71]. From book 10, introduced with ‘Yet’ against an impossibility she has stated, it teaches that one must enlarge the self beyond body and time to understand God, self-limitation being the obstacle and knowing, willing and hoping the way: “for the like is intelligible by the like” [III.3 ¶78; III.3 n51]. A passage cited with the Book of Wisdom (chap. 11, ver. 22) illustrates the world held before divine vision: “The whole world is before thee, O God! As a little grain of the balance” [III.3 ¶39; III.3 n26].

E1355.summary: An unnamed poet quoted for a line on the black soot bringing light and a phrase on the remoteness of the discovery.
E1355.body: An unnamed poet supplies a couplet illustrating that the black soot brings light: “Adferet haec Phoebi nigra favilla jubar.” [I.3 n22] (ours: ‘This black ash will bring the radiance of Phoebus’). Another phrase illustrates how remote the discovery is: “reclusa resedet longius” [III.1 ¶13] (ours, roughly: ‘withdrawn, it lies further off’).

E1356.summary: Poets in general, whose fables Atwood reads as veils of the vaporous estate, the Intelligible Sun, and receptive versus presumptuous approach.
E1356.body: Atwood reads the poets' Pan as a veil for the vaporous estate and its frightening disguises [II.3 ¶20]. Within the Platonic Successor's passage the Sun from which the Intelligible gods proceed is described as “emerging, as the Poets say, from the bosom of the ocean” [II.4 ¶41]. The stories of Actaeon and Endymion illustrate that presumptuous striving repels while sleeping receptivity receives the presence: “to the sleeping Endymion she vouchsafed her willing presence” [III.2 ¶57].

E1357.summary: Poets and traditionalists who, by the Walls of Troy built by Apollo's music, meant the insphering of the lower life (Appendix).
E1357.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Walls of Troy, said to be built by Apollo's music, are what the poets and traditionalists meant as a figure of the insphering of the lower life [APP ¶49].

E1358.summary: A point in the process with no attraction, only indifference to life and death, when the Artist must stir up the Motion.
E1358.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Alchemists, with Atwood's endorsement, say “there is a point of passivity” [APP ¶82]: a point in the process with no attraction but indifference to both life and death, at which the Artist must stir up the Motion.

E1359.summary: The adepts' name for what is entered for the dissolution, ‘the greatest poison’; the root of the Science is also called ‘a deadly poison’.
E1359.body: Atwood reports that the adepts call what is entered for the dissolution the greatest poison — “adepts describe it indeed as the greatest poison” [III.1 ¶56] — and that the root of the Science is called deadly: “because the root of this Science is a deadly poison” [III.1 ¶61]. The text does not say outright whether these are the same thing. Resolved into a subtle water, the poison coagulates our Mercury into silver [III.1 ¶56].

E1360.summary: In the Adept's loadstone figure, the point toward which the center turns, where the steel's virtue strengthens and the heart of the mercury, a true Fire, lies.
E1360.body: Speaking through a quoted Adept: “This center turns naturally towards the Pole where the virtue of the steel is gradually strengthened.” [IV.2 ¶30]; “In this Pole is the heart of the mercury, which is a true Fire” [IV.2 ¶30], in which its Lord rests. The figure is the loadstone and steel; its plain meaning is not stated in the record.

E1361.summary: The just weight or proportion in which, per Eirenaeus, the first water is joined to the body.
E1361.body: Quoting Eirenaeus: one is “to join it to the body in a just pondus” [III.1 ¶14] — the first water joined to the body in just weight or proportion.

E1362.summary: Author Atwood cites as a genuine seeker: he erred two hundred times, held the Fire the unrevealed key, and taught nothing in the subject is discarded.
E1362.body: Pontanus's Epistola appears to credit Artephius's tale [I.1 ¶36; I.1 n41]. He is listed with Rupicessa, De Meun, Flamel, Basil Valentine, Ripley, Lully and Cremer as genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49]. From his Epistle (Theat. Chem.) Atwood takes in support that he erred two hundred times, that the Fire is the unrevealed key found only by profound meditation: “seek to know this Fire with all thy soul” [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n40]. He also supports that nothing in the subject is to be discarded, superfluities being converted into essence by the Fire: “he who pretends to separate anything from our subject knows nothing of philosophy” [IV.3 ¶7].

E1363.summary: Something without which, along with Theurgic assistance, one cannot transcend the consciousness of this life; not explained further here.
E1363.body: Atwood writes: “Without the Pontic Medium, without Theurgic assistance we are unable to transcend the consciousness of this life” [II.4 ¶49]. The passage does not explain the term.

E1364.summary: The manner in which the Argent vive is generated: by a reciprocal alternation, passing its virtue hand to hand.
E1364.body: Atwood says the Argent vive “is generated pontically, as it were by a reciprocal alternation” [IV.1 ¶11], distributing its advanced virtue by hand to hand. Not otherwise explained.

E1365.summary: Eudoxus's name for the viscous liquor thickening under repeated affusion, also called Water of Life and the great Lunaria.
E1365.body: Quoting Eudoxus: “the philosophers give this viscous Liquor the name of Pontick Water” [IV.3 ¶9]; the liquor thickens under repeated affusion, and its exuberant ponticity is the character of its virtue. Asserted identities: = Water of Life — “It has been called the Water of Life, because it gives life to the metals” [IV.3 ¶9]; = great Lunaria — “it is properly called the great Lunaria, because of its brightness wherewith it shines” [IV.3 ¶9].

E1366.summary: Pope, whose Homer's Iliad Atwood quotes while criticizing his rendering of the heroic tears as ‘unavailing’.
E1366.body: Atwood quotes Pope's Iliad, book 18 — “Patroclus dead, Achilles hates to live.” [III.1 ¶29; III.1 n35] — and criticizes him for rendering the heroic tears ‘unavailing’ [III.1 ¶30].

E1367.summary: Pope said to have practised the art he interdicted and enriched the treasury by it.
E1367.body: Atwood reports that Pope John XXII is said to have practised the art he interdicted and enriched the treasury by it, illustrating its continued secret pursuit [I.1 ¶55].

E1368.summary: Pope's Homer's Odyssey, book 8, read as figuring the dominion of Intellect and the sea barring the goal.
E1368.body: Atwood quotes Pope's Odyssey, book 8 — “In wondrous ships self-moved, instinct with mind;” [IV.1 ¶20; IV.1 n20] — reading the Phoeacian ships and Alcinous' court as the dominion of Intellect and the vast sea as the barrier before the goal [IV.1 ¶21–24; IV.1 n21].

E1369.summary: Author of Mundorum Explicatoio, quoted for verse on the sphere where God displays himself to himself.
E1369.body: Atwood quotes Pordage's Mundorum Explicatoio (p. 320): “Here ‘tis that God himself t’ himself displays” [III.2 ¶18; III.2 n19], illustrating the sphere of divine self-display.

E1370.summary: A school Atwood says is not to be undervalued, on the same original track as Boehme.
E1370.body: Atwood says the Pordage and Lead school is not to be undervalued, being on the same original track as Boehme [I.1 ¶68].

E1371.summary: Neoplatonist whose Auxiliaries to Intelligibles and Cave of the Nymphs Atwood cites on purification, the twofold death, the soul's reunion with its source and pure Matter.
E1371.body: Named among the Alexandrian revival figures [I.1 ¶27], the Neoplatonists who dilate on the same ground [II.1 ¶39] and whose writings show the Mysteries [II.2 ¶9], and in the ‘golden chain of Hermetic philosophers’ who claimed Homer and Virgil as their own [III.1 ¶25]. His Auxiliaries supply a chapter motto: “It s necessary that the soul, when purified, should associate with its Generator.” [II.3 ¶2; cf. II.3 ¶43]. A moist spirit binds the soul to images and earth: “If the soul on its departure, says Porphyry, still possesses a spirit turbid from humid exhalations, it then attracts to itself a shadow and becomes heavy” [II.3 ¶27; II.3 n29]; leaving nature makes it a dry splendor. He explains the twofold death, which Atwood glosses — “the other peculiar to philosophers, in which the soul is liberated from the body” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n45]. His Hymn to Plotinus illustrates waking vision: “Nor was the vision like the dreams of sleep, But seen whilst vigilant you brave the deep” [II.3 ¶51; II.3 n57]. The Cave of the Nymphs supports the northern and southern gates as descent into generation and ascent to divinity [II.4 ¶7; II.4 n2]; the self-reflexive vision is “a fountain, not flowing outwardly, but circularly scattering its streams into itself” [II.4 ¶15; II.4 n6]. When discipline is complete “the motions themselves will be dissolved through their proximity to the reasoning power” [II.4 ¶36–37; II.4 n25]. Additions of place or selfhood veil the Eternal Essence; “being established in yourself and in your own Essence, you will be assimilated to the Intelligible Universe” [III.2 ¶59; III.2 n44]. With Plotinus he is co-source of the summary on pure Matter [III.2 ¶46], and ‘the Greek Porphyry’ appears in the Ammonius story [III.2 ¶64].

E1372.summary: A product which, like the philosophers' stone, takes its beginning from the divine water (per Hermolaus Barbarus).
E1372.body: Quoting Hermolaus Barbarus, the divine water is that “whence potable gold, and the stone of philosophers, takes its beginning” [I.1 ¶20].

E1373.summary: The transmuting agent in the Dee/Kelly story, found at Glastonbury and so strong its true height had to be found by trial.
E1373.body: In the Dee/Kelly story Atwood relates the finding of “a large quantity of the Powder of Projection in a niche amongst the ruins of Glastonbury Abbey” [I.1 ¶66]; it was so strong (1 upon 272,330) that its ‘true height’ had to be found by trial.

E1374.summary: Transmuting powder said by Dickenson to have been found in Lully's cell, enriching the workmen.
E1374.body: Per Dickenson, “a certain quantity of the powder of transmutation” [I.1 ¶47] was found in Lully's cell and enriched the workmen.

E1375.summary: What secrecy ensured could be discovered only by the long labour of an experienced, upright mind.
E1375.body: Atwood says secrecy was kept “that the Power might only be discovered through the long labour of an experienced and upright mind” [III.4 ¶9].

E1376.summary: The double capacity figured by Cheiron, who educates the Heroic Fire and rectifies the Armed Magnet.
E1376.body: Atwood describes Cheiron “in his double capacity of Power and Motive in alliance” [IV.1 ¶33], educating the Heroic Fire and rectifying the Armed Magnet.

E1377.summary: The Light shining in darkness within man, identified with the true Light; an enchanted treasury known only to the wisely simple.
E1377.body: Atwood: “This therefore is that Power which is hidden in man, the true Light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [II.3 ¶55] — thus = the true Light. It is “An enchanted treasury known only to the wisely simple” [II.3 ¶55].

E1378.summary: One of three modes of consciousness, with the sensible and perceptive, which conjoined to them makes them efficient (Appendix).
E1378.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood names three modes: “either in the sensible, the perceptive, or the power life; this last conjoined to the other two makes them efficient” [APP ¶45].

E1379.summary: The operative procedure of the Hermetic work, which Atwood seeks to understand rather than exhibit, touching only certain particulars.
E1379.body: Atwood distinguishes understanding from exhibiting the operative procedure: “But we are not yet proposing to exhibit the Practice, but only to understand it” [III.1 ¶56]. She sets out impediments and endowments “before we enter on the routine of Practice” [III.4 ¶2], and at the close says she has “suggested certain particulars concerning the Practice at this latter end” [IV.3 ¶54], which may be unfamiliar to the reader.

E1381.summary: Mother of Hippocrates, of the race of the Heraclides.
E1381.body: Named as Hippocrates' mother, of the race of the Heraclides [IV.3 ¶32].
